commitResults.messageTitle: Level-0: Rename Duke, add greeting and exit
commitResults.messageBody:
The template ships with a bare Duke class that only prints the setup banner and has no chatbot behavior yet.

Level-0 requires customizing the chatbot's name and giving it a basic greet/exit interaction.

The main class is renamed from Duke to Verity, prints a startup greeting, and exits with a farewell msg.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-1: Add echo of user input
commitResults.messageBody:
Verity currently only greets the user and exits immediately on bye; other input entered by the user is ignored.

Level-1 requires the chatbot to echo back whatever the user types until they exit.

Let's add a loop that reads each line of input, echoes it back between dividers, and repeats until bye is entered, at which point the existing farewell prints as before.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-2: Add task and list command
commitResults.messageBody:
Verity currently only echoes back whatever the user types and does not remember anything between commands.

Level-2 requires storing user-entered text and displaying it back when the user asks for it.

Let's add a fixed-size array to hold up to 100 tasks, store each non-command input in it while printing an added confirmation, and branch on the list command to print all stored tasks numbered from 1.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-3: Add mark and unmark commands
commitResults.messageBody:
Verity can store and list tasks but has no way to track whether a task is completed.

Level-3 requires the ability to mark tasks as done, and reverse that status.

Let's add mark and unmark commands that parse the task index from user input and flip a per-task done flag stored in a parallel boolean array, updating list to display [X] or [ ] based on that flag.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-3: Extract Task class (A-Classes)
commitResults.messageBody:
Task data is currently spread across two parallel arrays (String[] tasks and boolean[] isDone), with mark/unmark/list all indexing into both together.

Level-3's A-Classes extension asks for task state to be represented by a dedicated Task class instead of parallel primitive arrays.

Let's introduce a Task class encapsulating description and done-status, with markAsDone()/markAsNotDone() methods and a toString() that renders its own [X]/[ ] display line. Verity.java now stores a single Task[] array and delegates to these methods instead of manipulating two arrays in lockstep.

This is a pure refactor: command behavior and output are unchanged, only the internal representation improved, in line with the OOP approach the extension calls for.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add ToDo, Deadline, and Event task types
commitResults.messageBody:
Task list only supports generic tasks with a description and a
done status.

Users need to track tasks with different shapes: todos with no
date, deadlines with a single due date, and events with a start
and end time.

Let's add Todo, Deadline, and Event as subclasses of Task, each
overriding toString() to render its own type tag and date info,
and wire up todo/deadline/event commands in Verity to parse and
create them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add UI test plan and test-ui skill
commitResults.messageBody:
Manually re-testing console behavior after every change is slow
and easy to skip.

Let's record test cases in test/ui-test-plan.md and add a test-ui
skill that runs each command and checks the output against the
expected text.

This follows the module's AI Guidance to have the AI check its own
work, on top of manual testing.

commitResults.messageTitle: bug fix: Make /by, /from, /to markers case-insensitive
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadline and event commands split the input on the literal
markers /by, /from, and /to, matched case-sensitively.

A user who types the marker in a different case, e.g. /By or
/FROM, gets it treated as part of the description instead of
being recognized, so the date/time is silently dropped instead of
being an error.

Let's match the markers case-insensitively so the command works
regardless of how the user cases them.

This keeps the parser forgiving of minor input variation without
requiring users to remember exact casing for the markers.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-5: Add error handling for invalid commands and input
commitResults.messageBody:
Invalid inputs: an empty todo description, a deadline/event
missing its /by, /from, or /to marker, an out-of-range mark/unmark
index, or an unrecognized command, was either silently accepted
or handled inconsistently. An unrecognized command line was even
stored as a plain task instead of being flagged as a mistake.

Users had no way to tell why their input didn't do what they
expected.

Let's add a VerityException class, thrown by each parsing/
validation path with a message specific to that failure, and
catch it once in the main loop. Unrecognized commands now throw
instead of falling back to storing the raw line as a task.

A single checked exception type keeps validation cleanly separate
from command dispatch, and forces every parsing path to either
produce a valid task or a clear, specific explanation.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-6: Add Delete function
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks were stored in a fixed-size Task[100] array with a manual
taskCount counter tracked alongside it, so adding a task meant
remembering to keep two things in sync, and there was a hard cap
of 100 tasks.

There was also no way to delete a task once added, and the fixed
array made deletion awkward where removing an item would mean
manually shifting every later element down by hand.

Let's replace Task[] tasks and taskCount with a single
ArrayList<Task> (A-Collections), using its own size() everywhere
taskCount was used, and add a delete <task number> command built
on the existing parseTaskIndex helper so it gets the same empty/
non-numeric/out-of-range error handling as mark and unmark for
free.

ArrayList's remove(index) handles the element-shifting itself,
so delete needs no manual array bookkeeping, and dropping the
fixed capacity means the task list can no longer silently run
out of room.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Enums: Represent commands as an enum
commitResults.messageBody:
Commands were recognized with a chain of command.startsWith(...)
string checks, and the same command names appeared again as
literal strings in the invalid-command error message.

String checks for a fixed set of known values don't get any
compile-time safety -- a typo in a keyword, or forgetting to add
a new command to the invalid-command message, would only surface
as a runtime bug, not a compile error.

Let's introduce a Command enum with one constant per command
(LIST, TODO, DEADLINE, EVENT, MARK, UNMARK, DELETE, BYE), each
holding its own keyword and whether it takes arguments, with a
match() helper to resolve user input to a constant and a
describeAll() helper to build the invalid-command message's list
of valid commands from the enum itself.

This makes the switch on Command exhaustive and checked by the
compiler, and means a new command only needs to be added in one
place (the enum) instead of also being hand-added to the
invalid-command error message.

commitResults.messageTitle: Save tasks to disk on every change (write happy path)
Load tasks from disk on startup (read happy path)
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage.load() parses ./data/verity.txt back into Todo/Deadline/Event,
returning an empty list if the file doesn't exist yet (first run).

Also fix run_ui_tests.py: it runs each test case as a fresh process but
shares the repo's working directory, so saved tasks from one case were
leaking into the next via data/verity.txt. Wipe data/ before each case.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-7: Skip corrupted save-file lines instead of crashing
commitResults.messageBody:
parseTask() used to throw an unchecked IllegalStateException for an
unrecognized type, which crashed the whole app on startup if one line
in data/verity.txt was malformed. Add CorruptedSaveDataException (checked,
mirrors VerityException) and validate field count and the done-flag;
load() now catches it per line, warns, and skips just that line.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-7 into master
commitResults.messageBody: Level-7 (Save) is complete: tasks persist across runs via a Storage class, including graceful handling of a missing data file and corrupted save-file lines.

commitResults.messageTitle: Parse deadline/event dates as LocalDate
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadline.by and Event.from/to are now LocalDate instead of free-form
String. Accepts yyyy-MM-dd input (e.g. 2019-10-15), displays as
MMM dd yyyy (e.g. Oct 15 2019), per the spec's minimal example.

An unparseable date is rejected with a VerityException naming the
marker and value; a corrupted date in the save file is treated the
same as any other corrupted field (skip the line, warn, keep going).

Update ui-test-plan.md: every case using free-form dates (Sunday,
Mon 2pm, etc.) now uses valid yyyy-MM-dd input, and TC7b/TC8b gain
invalid-date-format cases.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-8: Add 'on <date>' to list tasks on a given date
commitResults.messageBody:
Stretch goal: on <yyyy-MM-dd> lists every deadline due, and every
event spanning, that date. A todo never matches (no date); a deadline
matches on exact due date; an event matches if the date falls within
its from/to range inclusive.

Add getBy()/getFrom()/getTo() to Deadline/Event so Verity reads dates
through accessors rather than the protected fields directly.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-8 into master
commitResults.messageBody: Level-8 (Dates and Times) is complete: deadline/event dates are parsed as LocalDate with yyyy-MM-dd input and MMM dd yyyy display, plus the 'on <date>' stretch goal to list tasks occurring on a given date.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-MoreOOP: Finish Command pattern extraction
commitResults.messageBody:
Verity handles command dispatch, argument parsing, and task-list mutation all in one static class, with Storage hardcoded to a single file path.

This increment asks for TaskList, Parser, and (as a stretch goal) a Command class hierarchy, so each concern gets its own class instead of being folded into Verity.

Let's add TaskList to own the task collection, make Storage instance-based by passing its file path to the constructor instead of hardcoding it, add Parser.parse() to turn one line of input into a Command object, and add a Command hierarchy (ListCommand, OnCommand, MarkCommand, UnmarkCommand, DeleteCommand, AddCommand, ExitCommand) each implementing its own execute(TaskList, Ui, Storage). The old Command enum is renamed to CommandWord to free up the name for the new abstract class, and Verity itself becomes an instance-based orchestrator whose constructor loads tasks, whose run() holds the read-parse-execute loop, and whose main() is one line.

Reusing a shared Command.requireValidIndex() helper keeps index-out-of-range handling consistent across every command instead of repeating the same check in each one, and matching the target example's naming and structure almost verbatim keeps the result recognizable against the spec.

All 21 UI test cases still pass; also manually re-checked divider placement, the save/load round trip, out-of-range index errors, and corrupted-save-file handling. One side effect of matching the example's constructor/run() split: a load-time corrupted-file warning now prints before the welcome banner instead of after.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Packages: Organize classes into verity.* packages
commitResults.messageBody:
All classes lived directly under src/main/java with no package declaration.

This increment asks for a suitable package structure, keeping src/main/java as the source root.

Let's split the classes into six packages along the seams already established during A-MoreOOP: verity (Verity, VerityException), verity.ui (Ui), verity.storage (Storage, CorruptedSaveDataException), verity.task (Task/Todo/Deadline/Event/TaskList), verity.parser (Parser, CommandWord), and verity.command (Command plus the seven concrete command classes).

verity.task depends on nothing else in the app, so every other package can depend on it without risking a cycle.

Fix one cross-package visibility break this surfaced: Task's DATE_DISPLAY_FORMAT was protected, but Ui (a different package, not a Task subclass) reads it directly - widened it to public, since it's a shared formatting constant, not sensitive state.

Update the test-ui harness's default main class from Verity to verity.Verity (script and SKILL.md), and fix the file path in README's setup instructions.

Verified: compiles cleanly, runs correctly as verity.Verity, and all 21 UI test cases still pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'add-gradle-support' into master
commitResults.messageBody: Adds Gradle build support (build.gradle, gradlew, gradle wrapper) provided by the course, so the project can later be built/run/tested through Gradle instead of manual javac invocations.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Gradle: Configure Gradle entry point and jar name
commitResults.messageBody: Configure build.gradle to use verity.Verity as the Gradle entry point instead of the Duke template's placeholder, and rename the shadowJar output to verity.jar. Verified that Gradle can build and run the project successfully.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-JUnit: Add tests for task/parser/command/storage logic
commitResults.messageBody:
No JUnit tests exist yet, even though build.gradle already has the JUnit dependencies wired up from the A-Gradle increment.

This increment's stretch goal asks for meaningful coverage of the codebase's more complex logic rather than trivial getter/setter tests, with roughly 50% coverage as the target.

Let's add 89 tests across 9 classes, prioritizing the logic most likely to break. Task/Todo/Deadline/Event cover done-status and the toString()/toSaveFormat() overrides. TaskList covers add/remove/isValidIndex boundaries, the unmodifiable list returned by getTasks(), and getTasksOnDate() across a deadline's exact match, an event's inclusive range boundaries, a todo that never matches, and mixed lists. Storage covers the save/load round trip, a missing file/folder, and every corrupted-line case, using @TempDir so tests never touch the real project's data folder. CommandWord covers exact vs. prefix keyword matching. Parser covers every command's valid and error paths, verified by executing the returned Command against a real TaskList rather than adding test-only getters to the Command subclasses. Command itself covers shared abstract-class behavior: singular/plural error wording, the save-failure warning path, and isExit() across every concrete command.

Ui is left untested: it's pure print formatting with no branching logic, lowest value relative to effort against the 50% target.

Update AGENTS.md (included by CLAUDE.md) to document the 50% coverage target and that tests should stay in sync as code changes, so this expectation persists into future sessions.

Verified: gradlew test (89/89 pass), gradlew build (full build succeeds), and the existing /test-ui console suite (21/21, no regression since no src/main code changed).

commitResults.messageTitle: A-JavaDoc: Add Javadoc to all non-private members
commitResults.messageBody:
83.3% of Task/Command/Parser/Storage's public and protected classes, methods, and constructors have Javadoc; 15 do not, all of them @Override methods that don't automatically inherit a parent comment describing their specific behavior.

The course's coding standard lets an override skip its own comment only when the parent's Javadoc already applies exactly as is. Command's abstract execute() only describes a generic contract, not what each concrete command actually does, so its seven overrides need their own summaries; Task's toString()/toSaveFormat() and Command's isExit(), by contrast, are already written generically enough to apply to every override verbatim.

Let's write a distinct summary sentence for each Command subclass's execute(), reusing {@inheritDoc} only for the @param entries whose descriptions genuinely don't change per command; use bare {@inheritDoc} on the toString()/toSaveFormat()/isExit() overrides where the parent's doc already covers them; add Javadoc to main() and every CommandWord enum constant; and add one-line field comments to Task/Deadline/Event's instance fields.

Coverage confirmed at 100% (90/90) via a script auditing every non-private class/method/constructor for a preceding Javadoc block, cross-checked by hand against every {@inheritDoc} use to confirm the parent's comment genuinely applies. javadoc itself reports zero errors, and all 21 existing UI tests still pass, confirming this is a pure documentation change.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-CodingStandard: Add seedu-java-coding-standard skill
commitResults.messageBody:
No project-specific reference for the SE-EDU Java coding standard exists, so following it consistently in every future edit relies on memory rather than a checkable reference.

A-CodingStandard requires all Java code, including code written after this increment, to follow the standard's basic and intermediate rules.

Let's add a seedu-java-coding-standard skill summarizing the standard's naming, layout, control-flow, import, and Javadoc rules, sourced from the SE-EDU Java coding standard guide, so it can be consulted and applied consistently going forward.

Keeping this as a skill rather than inline text in AGENTS.md keeps the full rule set available without bloating the always-loaded agent file.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-CodingStandard: Add seedu-git-standard skill
commitResults.messageBody:
No project-specific reference for the SE-EDU Git commit-message and branch-naming conventions exists either, with the same risk of drifting from the standard over time.

A-CodingStandard requires commit message subjects to follow the SE-EDU Git conventions guide, with the body conventions applying whenever a body is included.

Let's add a seedu-git-standard skill covering the subject-line rules, the optional body structure, and branch-naming conventions, sourced from the SE-EDU Git conventions guide.

Every commit from Level-7 onward has already followed this structure informally; this just makes the rule set explicit and checkable instead of relying on memory of past commits.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-CodingStandard: Wire new skills into AGENTS.md
commitResults.messageBody:
AGENTS.md doesn't yet point at the seedu-java-coding-standard or seedu-git-standard skills just added, so nothing tells future sessions to actually use them.

A skill that exists but isn't referenced from the agent file won't reliably get applied.

Let's add a Coding standard section mandating seedu-java-coding-standard for every Java edit, and update the Git section to point at seedu-git-standard for every commit message.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-CodingStandard: Reindent switches, wrap long lines
commitResults.messageBody:
Parser.java and Storage.java's switch statements indent case labels at the same level as switch, matching IntelliJ's default but not the SE-EDU standard's template. Two exception messages in Parser.java also exceed the standard's 120-character hard limit.

A-CodingStandard requires the codebase to comply with the basic and intermediate SE-EDU Java coding standard from this point on.

Let's reindent both switch statements so case sits one level deeper than switch, per the standard's template; add the required // Fallthrough comment where case BYE falls through to default with no break; and rewrap the two over-length exception messages across multiple lines, breaking before the string-concatenation operator and indenting continuations 8 spaces, per the standard's line-wrapping rules.

Confirmed no line in the codebase exceeds 120 characters, all 21 UI test cases pass unchanged, and the project compiles clean - these are formatting-only changes with zero logic altered.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-9: Add find command to search task descriptions
commitResults.messageBody:
There is no way to search the task list; finding a specific task means reading through the entire numbered list by eye.

Let's add a find command: FindCommand executes against a new TaskList.findByKeyword(keyword) method, matching any task whose description contains the keyword, case-insensitively. Ui's new showMatchingTasks() reports the results using the wording from the spec's own example.

Adding FIND to the CommandWord enum changed describeAll()'s output, which broke an existing hardcoded test - fixed alongside the new tests, as a direct consequence of this change rather than a separate concern.

Verified: the full 24-case /test-ui console suite passes (21 existing plus 3 new for find), the project compiles clean, and javadoc reports no errors on the new {@inheritDoc} usage in FindCommand. Could not run gradlew test in this session (no network access to Maven Central here) - worth a real run to confirm the new JUnit tests pass too.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-CheckStyle: Set up Checkstyle and fix flagged violations
commitResults.messageBody:
This project already follows the seedu-java-coding-standard skill by convention, but nothing mechanically checks that new code actually complies - style drift can only be caught by manual review.

This increment asks whether Checkstyle adds value alongside the skill. It does: the skill guides how code gets written in the first place, but only a tool like Checkstyle catches a violation that slips through anyway, on every build, without relying on remembering to check.

Let's add the checkstyle Gradle plugin, using the same config from AddressBook-Level3 that's built to match this exact coding standard, and fix the two violations it flags: three lambda expressions in CommandTest.java and one Parser.parse() call in ParserTest.java exceeded the 120-character line limit once wrapped onto a single line. Extracting a newStorage() helper in CommandTest and an input variable in ParserTest keeps each line short without splitting the assertion itself across lines.

Verified: compiles clean, all 24 existing UI tests still pass, and Checkstyle reports zero violations across the whole source tree, confirmed by running the standalone Checkstyle 14.1.0 JAR directly against config/checkstyle/checkstyle.xml (sanity-checked by deliberately introducing a violation and confirming it gets caught). Still worth running ./gradlew checkstyleMain checkstyleTest directly to confirm the Gradle-integrated path behaves the same way.
